assessment.nobel_worthiness: Collateral constraints that amplify and propagate shocks (Kiyotaki-Moore) and the financial accelerator (Bernanke-Gertler lineage) are core building blocks of modern macro-finance. They changed how macroeconomists model credit, asset prices and downturns, and they shaped policy thinking after 2008.
assessment.attribution: The Kiyotaki-Moore credit-cycles model is the clearest single origin. Gertler's work spans the accelerator and later quantitative and policy extensions. Gilchrist's contributions are important but more empirical and derivative. Bernanke's earlier prize covers part of the accelerator lineage, so the credited set should centre on Kiyotaki, Moore and Gertler.
assessment.maturity: The foundational papers date from 1989-1999 and have decades of confirmation in theory, quantitative models and central-bank practice. The 2022 prize partly covered the adjacent banking and financial-crisis area, but this is a distinct contribution.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize and with Gertler's role in the Bernanke-Gertler framework may affect how the Committee judges novelty.
Empirical evidence on the strength of the accelerator is mixed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Random-coefficients demand estimation (BLP) and dynamic industry models made empirical industrial organisation credible and quantitative. They are used throughout merger review, antitrust, regulation and trade, and they have had very large methodological and practical impact.
assessment.attribution: Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes (1995) is the identifiable core, with Berry's earlier logit-inversion paper and Pakes's dynamic-game and Ericson-Pakes work. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin are significant but have narrower or less central credit, and the three-laureate cap forces exclusions.
assessment.maturity: Thirty years of use and extensions, including identification and computational critiques, indicate a mature and robust contribution. It has no prior Nobel overlap.
uncertainties: Choosing three among a broad structural-IO group is difficult, and Bresnahan's role is arguably underweighted.
Structural assumptions and identification debates remain active.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The alternating-offers bargaining model gave the canonical non-cooperative foundation for bargaining and a sharp link to the Nash solution. It underpins work in contract theory, market design, political economy, labour and macro search models.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein (1982) is the central contribution. Rubinstein-Wolinsky extended it to decentralised markets. Binmore's related contributions (the Nash program and the 1986 joint work) are real but secondary, which supports a two-person credit.
assessment.maturity: The result is more than forty years old and thoroughly absorbed into the canon. Game theory has been recognised repeatedly, but bargaining theory itself has not.
uncertainties: Whether Binmore merits inclusion, and the right credit split between the 1982 model and the market-bargaining extensions.
Game theory has had several prizes, so the Committee may prefer other fields.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Political economics of constitutions, electoral rules, state capacity and fiscal policy is a central integrative contribution, with formal models and empirical tests of how institutions shape policy and outcomes. Its influence extends well into comparative politics.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the joint authors of the field-defining synthesis and the constitutional-design and electoral-rule work. Besley contributes accountability, state capacity and development-linked political economy. The three-way credit is plausible, though other contributors exist.
assessment.maturity: The work spans the mid-1990s to the 2010s and is well confirmed, including by natural experiments and cross-country evidence. The 2024 prize on institutions is thematically adjacent, which may lower the marginal case.
uncertainties: Disclosure: Torsten Persson is a past co-author of mine (with Rothstein, on corruption), and my field is adjacent. I am not adjudicating this conflict here.
Thematic proximity to the 2024 prize may weigh against timing.
Identification in cross-country constitutional comparisons is sometimes weak.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities, staggered pricing and contracts, policy rules and the micro-founded New Keynesian framework are the working language of modern monetary policy analysis and central-bank practice.
assessment.attribution: The credit is highly diffuse: Calvo (pricing), Taylor (staggered contracts and the rule), Woodford (synthesis and optimal policy), Galí, and Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans (DSGE estimation) are all strong. Any three-person selection leaves out highly deserving contributors, which weakens attribution clarity.
assessment.maturity: The ideas are thirty to forty years old and fully institutionalised. Their post-2008 and post-2021 performance has led to critiques and extensions.
uncertainties: Heavy attribution ambiguity and the arbitrary three-person cut.
Challenges to the framework from the 2008 crisis and the 2021-23 inflation episode.
Partial overlap with the contributions of earlier laureates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Evidence on trade shocks, technology and tasks reshaped understanding of labour-market adjustment, polarisation and the political consequences of globalisation. It has major policy and public-debate influence and strong empirical design.
assessment.attribution: The China-shock work (Autor-Dorn-Hanson) is clearly credited. The task-based framework with Katz and Murphy is partly distinct and overlaps with Acemoglu's prize-winning work, so I propose the China-shock trio.
assessment.maturity: The central results date from 2013 onward, and the literature is still debating magnitudes and persistence. Maturity is moderate and the long-run assessment is pending.
uncertainties: Replication and reinterpretation of the long-run labour-market effects of import competition.
Overlap with the task and technology work recognised in 2024.
Whether the Committee prefers to wait.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The misallocation framework quantified how distortions in resource allocation across firms explain a large share of cross-country TFP differences. It created a major research programme in growth, development and macro.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh-Klenow (2009) is the core paper. Restuccia-Rogerson (2008) is a near-simultaneous parallel contribution. Credit therefore has a real multiple-discovery issue, and the cap forces a choice.
assessment.maturity: It is fifteen to eighteen years old and heavily used. Measurement critiques (such as measurement error and the role of markups) are ongoing.
uncertainties: Whether Restuccia, or Rogerson (who is not listed), should be credited alongside Hsieh and Klenow.
Sensitivity of the measured misallocation to data quality and modelling assumptions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting transformed the theory and empirics of trade by shifting the gains from trade to within-industry reallocation. It is the dominant framework in the field after the New Trade Theory.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the clear core. Helpman's contributions include Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple and a wide body of trade theory. Redding's later quantitative work is valuable but derivative. Krugman's prior prize covered an earlier stage of trade theory.
assessment.maturity: The framework is more than twenty years old with large empirical support, and subsequent quantitative work has refined it.
uncertainties: Trade has had relatively recent recognition, and Helpman's credit may be better placed in a broader trade-and-growth citation.
Whether quantitative-trade work (Eaton-Kortum) should be considered alongside Melitz.
